_meta.title: Ke Aupuni O Ke Akua — Mistranslations Lexicon
_meta.description: Words from the original Biblical Hebrew, Biblical Aramaic, and Koine Greek where common English translations flatten, lose, or invert the descriptive meaning. Every entry keyed by Strong's number. The author field marks which entries are Kahu's own work and which are drafts awaiting his review.
_meta.copyright: © Ke Aupuni O Ke Akua Press. All entries retain copyright.

G25.actual_meaning: To love — but not merely affection or friendship. In classical Greek agapaō meant to be well-pleased, to be contented with. In the NT it carries the weight of a deliberate, self-giving commitment that chooses the well-being of another regardless of response. Distinguished from phileō (emotional fondness) and erōs (desire). God's agapaō of the world (John 3:16) is covenantal, volitional love.
G25.why_mistranslated: Modern English 'love' collapses at least four distinct Greek words into one. The deliberate, covenantal dimension of agapaō is lost — readers hear 'God loved the world' as warm feeling instead of sovereign, committed self-giving.
G25.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G26.actual_meaning: Love — the defining NT word for God's own nature and the command to imitate it. Not sentiment but the steady, purposeful goodwill that seeks the highest good of the beloved. Thayer: 'the deepest and most spiritual of the words for love.' Unlike eros (desire) or philia (friendship/kinship affection), agapē can be commanded because it is a choice, not merely a feeling.
G26.why_mistranslated: English 'love' cannot bear the covenantal weight. Agapē is commandable; feelings are not. Translation collapses this distinction and makes Jesus's commands sound impossible or shallow.
G26.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G932.english_flattened: kingdom (as a place you enter after death)
G932.actual_meaning: Kingdom, reign, royal rule. Not primarily a territory but the active RULE of a king. Basileia tou Theou = the sovereign reign of God breaking into history. Thayer: 'royal power, kingship, dominion, rule.' Jesus uses it almost entirely in the dynamic sense — God's rule arriving, invading, transforming — not a static territory people enter after death.
G932.why_mistranslated: Western political frameworks imported a static 'kingdom-as-place' meaning. Readers hear 'kingdom of heaven' and think of a location rather than the active reign of God breaking in. This single mistranslation has shaped Western Christianity away from Jesus's actual teaching.
G932.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G935.actual_meaning: King — the supreme ruler. In NT context, the title given to God and to Christ as His anointed representative. The word implies absolute sovereign authority, not the constitutional/limited monarchy of modern thought.
G935.why_mistranslated: Modern readers picture ceremonial European monarchs. The NT basileus is war-leader, judge, priest, and representative of the divine rolled into one. The weight of 'Christ is King' is lost when readers hear it through post-Enlightenment monarchy imagery.
G935.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4151.actual_meaning: Spirit, wind, breath. The range of meaning is significant: (1) wind/breath — physical moving air, (2) the animating life-principle in a person, (3) a spiritual being, (4) the Holy Spirit. Context determines which. In John 3:8, Jesus deliberately plays on all the meanings: 'The pneuma blows where it wills... so is everyone born of the pneuma.' The original audience would feel the layered meaning.
G4151.why_mistranslated: 'Ghost' in KJV English now means apparition of the dead. 'Spirit' has become disembodied abstraction. The breath/wind dimension — the same word that describes God's breath in Genesis 2:7 — is lost. Readers miss that Jesus is making a physical pun in John 3.
G4151.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G2222.actual_meaning: Life — but specifically the life that belongs to God, divine life, life in its fullest and highest form. Distinguished from bios (G979), which means biological/physical life or livelihood. Zōē aiōnios ('eternal life') does not primarily mean 'life that goes on forever' but 'the life characteristic of the age to come' — God's own quality of life. John uses zōē almost exclusively for this divine, abundant life.
G2222.why_mistranslated: Greek has two words for life (zōē and bios); English has one. The NT's distinction between ordinary biological life and God's own quality of life collapses. 'Eternal life' gets read as duration when the primary meaning is QUALITY — God's kind of life, here now.
G2222.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G165.actual_meaning: Age, era, epoch — a period of time with its own character. NOT simply 'forever.' Aiōnios (the adjective) means 'belonging to the age [to come]' more than 'never-ending.' Thayer: 'a period of time of significant character; the world.' In rabbinic thought there were two ages: ha-olam hazeh (this present age) and ha-olam ha-ba (the age to come). Jesus announced the age to come was arriving.
G165.why_mistranslated: Translating aiōn/aiōnios as 'eternal/forever' imports Greek philosophical ideas of timeless duration. The Hebrew-rooted NT concept is about QUALITY of age, not infinite time. Major theological confusions about 'eternal punishment' and 'eternal life' trace back to this flattening.
G165.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4982.actual_meaning: To save, to rescue, to heal, to make whole. Critically: the word covers healing the sick just as much as rescuing from sin. When Jesus 'saves' someone in the Gospels, the same word is used for both healing the body and forgiving sin — because salvation in the Hebrew/Greek mindset was WHOLENESS, shalom, restoration of the whole person. Not just a ticket to heaven.
G4982.why_mistranslated: Evangelical English narrowed 'saved' to mean 'going to heaven when you die.' The Koine sōzō is holistic: physical healing, social restoration, forgiveness, deliverance from danger. The woman with the bleeding was 'saved' (healed). Blind Bartimaeus was 'saved' (given sight). Collapsing sōzō to eternal salvation loses the gospel's wholeness.
G4982.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G3056.actual_meaning: Word, reason, account, meaning. One of the most theologically loaded words in the NT. In Greek philosophy (Heraclitus, Stoics), Logos was the rational principle ordering the universe. In Jewish thought (Philo), it was the intermediary between God and creation. John 1:1 takes all these layers and says: This Logos is a Person, and He became flesh. The word carries the sense of the articulated mind, the expressed thought, the rational order behind everything.
G3056.why_mistranslated: English 'word' is a label for a spoken sound. Logos is the ORDERING REASON behind reality, the expressed mind of God. When John 1:1 reads 'In the beginning was the Word,' readers hear 'utterance' when they should hear 'the reasoning, ordering intelligence of God made personal.'
G3056.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G5485.actual_meaning: Grace, favor, goodwill. In classical Greek: that which brings joy, a pleasing quality, gratitude. In the NT it becomes the specific word for God's unearned, freely-given favor toward humanity. NOT 'unmerited favor' merely in the sense that we don't deserve it — the Greek carries the additional sense that it flows from the JOYFUL generosity of the giver, not from any calculation of worthiness.
G5485.why_mistranslated: 'Unmerited favor' makes grace transactional — 'I don't deserve it but God gives it anyway.' The Greek is relational: grace flows from God's own joy in giving, not from an assessment of our worthiness. The giver's gladness is the engine.
G5485.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G4102.actual_meaning: Faith, trust, faithfulness. This is crucial: pistis is NOT merely intellectual belief. It is the trust that emerges from being persuaded, from evidence. It carries the relational dimension of faithfulness/loyalty (like a treaty). Abraham's pistis was acting on what God said — it was trust that moved his feet. Often translated 'faith' but 'allegiance' or 'covenant loyalty' captures dimensions the English word loses.
G4102.why_mistranslated: Modern English 'faith' has drifted toward 'belief without evidence.' Biblical pistis is trust born from evidence, expressed through loyalty, demonstrated through action. Hebrews 11 is not about sincere belief — it's about people who acted on what God said.
G4102.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H4428.actual_meaning: King. The ancient Near Eastern concept of a king was very different from modern constitutional monarchy. A melek was the military leader, the supreme judge, the high priest's counterpart, and the representative of the divine before the people. In Israel, the earthly melek was always supposed to be subordinate to YHWH, the true Melek. The prophets constantly judged Israel's kings by whether they ruled as YHWH's viceroys or set themselves up as autonomous.
H4428.why_mistranslated: Modern ceremonial-monarch imagery replaces the ancient reality of the king as war-leader, judge, and divine representative. The theological weight of 'YHWH is King' loses its bite when readers imagine a crown and throne instead of sovereign active rule.
H4428.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H4438.actual_meaning: Kingdom, kingship, royal dominion. Like the Greek basileia, this word emphasizes the RULE more than the territory. The Aramaic equivalent malkuta is used in Daniel. In the Kaddish prayer (ancient Jewish liturgy), 'May His kingdom/malkuth come' is the same concept Jesus picks up in the Lord's Prayer — the active, transforming reign of God breaking into human affairs.
H4438.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as basileia. 'Kingdom' in English points to a place; malkuth points to active rule. When the Lord's Prayer says 'thy kingdom come,' Jesus is praying for God's RULE to arrive and transform — not for believers to be transported to a location.
H4438.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H7307.actual_meaning: Spirit, wind, breath. The exact parallel to Greek pneuma. Ruach Elohim in Genesis 1:2 — 'the Spirit/Wind/Breath of God' hovered over the waters. The same word describes the life-giving breath God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7 uses neshamah but ruach carries the same idea). Ezekiel 37: God tells the ruach to breathe into the dry bones. The word is inseparable from life, movement, power, and divine presence.
H7307.why_mistranslated: English has separate words for 'spirit,' 'wind,' and 'breath' — treating them as different categories. Hebrew sees them as one reality. When Genesis says 'the ruach of God moved,' readers miss the layered physicality. God's breath is God's wind is God's Spirit.
H7307.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H2617.actual_meaning: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty, lovingkindness. One of the most untranslatable Hebrew words. No English word captures it alone. BDB: 'goodness, kindness, faithfulness.' It is the love that holds to a covenant even when the other party has broken it. It is YHWH's defining characteristic — the love He showed Israel not because they deserved it but because He committed Himself. Translated 'mercy,' 'lovingkindness,' 'steadfast love,' 'loyalty,' 'grace' in various versions — none is adequate alone.
H2617.why_mistranslated: Every English rendering picks up one dimension and loses the others. 'Mercy' loses the covenant loyalty. 'Lovingkindness' loses the weight. 'Steadfast love' loses the relational commitment. Chesed is all of it at once — and the OT's repeated claim that YHWH's defining characteristic is chesed never lands in English.
H2617.root: possibly related to chasad — to bow down in kindness
H2617.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H6666.actual_meaning: Righteousness, justice — but in the RELATIONAL sense of being in right relationship with others and with God, fulfilling covenant obligations. This is NOT primarily forensic (legal standing) as later Western theology made it. In the OT, tsedaqah means doing right by the poor, the widow, the orphan, the foreigner — it is SOCIAL JUSTICE and COVENANT FAITHFULNESS combined. Abraham 'believed God and it was counted to him as tsedaqah' — meaning he was in right relationship with God.
H6666.why_mistranslated: Western theology (especially post-Reformation) made 'righteousness' mean legal standing before God. The OT meaning is relational and social — doing right by the vulnerable, keeping covenant. When the prophets cry for 'righteousness,' they mean justice for the poor, not individuals attaining moral purity.
H6666.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H7965.actual_meaning: Peace — but the Hebrew concept is FAR richer than the absence of conflict. Shalom is wholeness, completeness, flourishing, right relationships, well-being of the whole person and community. BDB: 'completeness, soundness, welfare, peace.' When the prophets speak of the Prince of Shalom (Isaiah 9:6), they mean the one who will restore total flourishing — economically, relationally, spiritually, physically. The Greek eirēnē (peace) translates it but loses much.
H7965.why_mistranslated: English 'peace' is negative — the absence of war. Shalom is positive — the presence of whole flourishing. The Messianic hope of shalom is not just 'no more fighting' but complete restoration of all things to thriving relationship.
H7965.root: shalem — to be whole, to be complete
H7965.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H1285.actual_meaning: Covenant. The foundational relational-legal concept of the OT. A berith was a solemn binding agreement, usually between unequals, establishing obligations, identity, and relationship. Covenants in the ANE were 'cut' (hence 'cut a covenant') — animals were slaughtered and the parties walked between the pieces, symbolizing: 'may this happen to me if I break these terms.' God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the New Covenant are all berith — God binding Himself to humanity.
H1285.why_mistranslated: Modern 'covenant' sounds like a legal contract or corporate agreement. Berith is relational, blood-sealed, identity-forming. When Scripture says God 'cut a covenant' with Abraham, readers miss the slaughtered animals, the walk between the pieces, the self-curse if the covenant is broken.
H1285.root: uncertain — possibly bara (to cut) or baru (Akkadian: bond)
H1285.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H8451.actual_meaning: Instruction, teaching, direction — not primarily 'law' in the modern legal sense. Torah comes from the verb yarah (to throw, to shoot, to point) — the idea of aiming, directing, teaching the way. The Torah is God's teaching on how to live, not a legal code to be enforced. Psalm 119 loves the Torah as instruction and delight, not as legal burden.
H8451.why_mistranslated: Translating torah as 'law' imports Roman and Enlightenment concepts of statutory legislation. The Hebrew is closer to 'instruction' or 'teaching' — the guidance of a parent or shepherd, not the pronouncement of a court. Paul's critique of 'works of the law' makes different sense when torah means 'instruction' instead of 'legal code.'
H8451.root: yarah — to throw, to shoot, to point
H8451.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H430.actual_meaning: God. The grammatically plural form used with singular verbs when referring to YHWH. In polytheistic contexts it can refer to gods (plural). For Israel: the one God in the fullness of His being. BDB: 'rulers, judges, divine ones, angels, gods, God.' The plural of majesty or fullness — the same pattern as Hebrew mayim (waters) being plural though often singular in meaning. Ancient Jewish and Christian interpreters saw hints of the Trinitarian fullness here.
H430.why_mistranslated: Translating as singular 'God' loses the plural-of-fullness nuance. The grammatical choice matters theologically — elohim with singular verbs preserves both unity and fullness in a way 'God' alone does not.
H430.pos: noun masculine plural (used with singular verbs for the one God)
H430.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3068.actual_meaning: The LORD. The personal covenant name of God, never merely a title. God revealed this name to Moses at the burning bush: 'I AM WHO I AM' / 'I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE' (Exodus 3:14). The name is connected to the Hebrew verb 'to be' — suggesting self-existence, eternal presence, and the God who shows up and acts. Jewish tradition calls this the Tetragrammaton (four letters: YHWH) and considered it too holy to pronounce. English Bibles substitute 'LORD' (all caps) following this tradition.
H3068.why_mistranslated: Substituting 'LORD' turns the personal name into a title. YHWH is to Elohim as 'Philip' is to 'pastor.' When Exodus says 'I am YHWH your Elohim,' it's saying 'I am Yahweh, your God' — name + title. Rendering both as 'the LORD your God' loses the intimate naming that defines covenant relationship.
H3068.root: hayah — to be, to exist, to become
H3068.pos: proper noun — the personal name of God
H3068.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H2421.actual_meaning: To live, to have life, to revive, to give life. This is the root behind chayim (life — always plural in Hebrew, suggesting life in its fullness and multiplicity). BDB: 'to live, to have life, to remain alive, to sustain life, to live prosperously, to revive, to be healed.' In Deuteronomy 30:19, 'choose life' uses this root — it means choose the whole flourishing that comes with covenant faithfulness.
H2421.why_mistranslated: English 'live' means biological survival. Hebrew chayah means flourishing — relational, economic, spiritual, physical thriving. 'Choose life' in Deut 30:19 is not 'avoid death' but 'choose the whole flourishing that covenant with God brings.'
H2421.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

H3519.actual_meaning: Glory, honor, weight, abundance. The original meaning is HEAVINESS or WEIGHT — what has substance, what is weighty and real. YHWH's kabod is His weighty, substantial, overwhelming presence and splendor. BDB: 'abundance, honor, glory.' When Isaiah says 'the whole earth is full of His glory' (6:3), he means the earth is laden, weighty, full of the presence of God. The NT equivalent is the Greek doxa.
H3519.why_mistranslated: English 'glory' has become religious jargon — vague, ethereal, light-show. Kabod is WEIGHT. Substance. Pressing, undeniable presence. When Moses asked to see God's kabod, he was asking to feel the weight of God's reality. The word teaches a physics of the divine.
H3519.root: kabad — to be heavy, to be weighty
H3519.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

A4437.actual_meaning: Kingdom, royal dominion. The Aramaic equivalent of Hebrew malkuth. Used extensively in Daniel where the shift from Hebrew to Aramaic signals a message for all nations, not just Israel. Daniel's four kingdoms and the 'kingdom of the Most High' (Daniel 7:27) use this word. The Kaddish prayer — which Jesus almost certainly knew — uses malkuth: 'May His kingdom be established.' This is the backdrop for the Lord's Prayer.
A4437.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as Hebrew malkuth and Greek basileia. The Aramaic shifts in Daniel signal a universal message; rendering as static 'kingdom' obscures both the rule/reign emphasis and the cross-linguistic continuity.
A4437.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

A426.actual_meaning: God. The Aramaic form of the Hebrew El/Elohim. Used in Daniel and Ezra where those books shift to Aramaic. Nebuchadnezzar uses this word when he recognizes God after his madness (Daniel 4:2). The same root appears in the Arabic Allah.
A426.why_mistranslated: Translating simply as 'God' loses the cross-Semitic continuity. Elah, Eloah, Elohim, Allah — all share the same Semitic root for deity. When Daniel's pagan kings recognize 'the God of heaven,' the shared-root word carries weight that a bare English 'God' cannot.
A426.author: Kahu Phil Stephens

G1525.actual_meaning: To come into, to go into, to enter INTO the experience of. Composite of eis (into) + erchomai (come/go). Carries the sense not just of crossing a threshold but of entering into participation, being absorbed into the reality of what is being entered. When Jesus says 'enter the Kingdom' (Matt 18:3, 19:23-24), He means enter INTO the experience of God's reign — not walk through a door into a place. To enter a gym is not the same as to enter the experience of training.
G1525.why_mistranslated: English 'enter' is referential — a line crossed, a door passed. Eiserchomai is descriptive — entering INTO the experiential reality. Jesus is not asking whether you'll make it through the turnstile at death but whether you'll let the Kingdom shape you now. The mistranslation turns the gospel of transformation into a gospel of admission.
G1525.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G3340.actual_meaning: To change one's mind — but far deeper than emotional regret. Meta (after, change) + noeō (to think, to perceive). A complete reorientation of mind, perception, and life direction. John the Baptist's and Jesus's opening message (Matt 3:2, 4:17) was not 'feel sorry for your sins' but 'reorient everything, because the Kingdom is arriving.' Repentance is turning, not weeping.
G3340.why_mistranslated: Latin Vulgate translated metanoeō as 'paenitentiam agite' ('do penance'), which shaped Western understanding toward sorrow and ritual. But the Greek is cognitive and volitional — change your mind, reorient your life. The evangelical 'feel bad about your sins' picture is a distant descendant of the original Koine call to wholesale life-direction change.
G3340.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G1577.actual_meaning: Called-out assembly. In classical Greek, the ekklēsia was the civic assembly of a Greek city — the citizens called out of their homes to gather for governance and decision-making. Jesus's choice of this word (Matt 16:18) is deliberately political: His followers are a counter-civic assembly, the called-out citizens of the Kingdom. NOT a building. NOT a denomination. NOT a religious organization. A gathered, governing community of Kingdom citizens.
G1577.why_mistranslated: English 'church' (from kuriakon, 'belonging to the Lord,' referring to buildings) reversed the meaning. Ekklēsia went from 'called-out civic assembly' to 'sacred building,' then to 'denomination.' Western Christianity has spent 1,800 years confusing the building, the institution, and the gathered people who ARE the ekklēsia.
G1577.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G1343.actual_meaning: Righteousness, justice, right-relationship. The Greek equivalent of Hebrew tsedaqah. Carries both the legal/forensic sense (being declared right) AND the relational/ethical sense (being in right relationship, doing right by others). Paul's usage in Romans has both dimensions — declaration by God, and the resulting lived right-relationship.
G1343.why_mistranslated: Post-Reformation theology emphasized the forensic/legal meaning ('declared righteous') at the expense of the relational/ethical. When Jesus says 'seek first the Kingdom and His dikaiosynē' (Matt 6:33), He means seek God's just-order in all relationships — not seek legal standing alone.
G1343.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G40.actual_meaning: Set apart, dedicated, distinct. The root idea is not moral purity but SEPARATION — something set apart for a specific purpose. The Hebrew equivalent qadosh carries the same emphasis. God is hagios because He is absolutely distinct from creation; saints (hagioi) are 'set-apart ones,' not necessarily morally superior. The word describes category, not quality.
G40.why_mistranslated: English 'holy' has come to mean moral perfection or religious superiority ('holier than thou'). The Greek is about SEPARATION and DEDICATION. Paul calls all believers 'hagioi' (saints, set-apart ones) — not because they're morally perfect but because they're dedicated to God's purposes.
G40.root: hagos — religious awe / that which is reverenced
G40.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H6918.actual_meaning: Set apart, separate, distinct. Same root idea as Greek hagios. YHWH is qadosh (holy) because He is absolutely other, absolutely distinct from creation. The seraphim cry 'qadosh, qadosh, qadosh' (Isa 6:3) — 'set-apart, set-apart, set-apart.' Israel is called to be qadosh not because they earn moral superiority but because they are dedicated to YHWH's purposes.
H6918.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as hagios. 'Holy' has come to mean moral perfection. Qadosh means categorically distinct. When God says 'be holy as I am holy,' He's not demanding perfection — He's calling Israel to the same dedicated, distinct way of life that reflects His own distinct character.
H6918.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G266.actual_meaning: Missing the mark. Archery imagery — an arrow that fails to hit the target. Hamartia is not primarily about moral transgression but about FAILURE TO REACH the intended purpose. Humans were created for a target (God's image, right relationship, flourishing); sin is any failure to hit that target — whether by rebellion, ignorance, weakness, or drift.
G266.why_mistranslated: English 'sin' has become a legal/moral category — a crime committed against God's rules. Hamartia is missing the point of what humans were made for. The difference matters: sin as 'rule-breaking' demands punishment; sin as 'missing the target' calls for reorientation. Jesus's way of speaking about sin aligns more with the archery picture than the courtroom.
G266.root: a- (not) + meros (a part, share) — to fail to share in, to miss
G266.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G3788.actual_meaning: Eye — but in Semitic thought behind the Greek (Matt 6:22-23), the eye is the window of perception and generosity. A 'good eye' (ophthalmos haplous) is a generous, single-focused eye; a 'bad eye' (ophthalmos ponēros) is a stingy, envious one. This is Jewish idiom imported into Greek. Jesus's teaching about the 'single eye' is not about literal vision but about generous, undivided attention.
G3788.why_mistranslated: English readers take 'if thine eye be single' literally or as mystical spiritual vision. The Jewish idiom is about generosity of spirit and undivided focus. Jesus is warning against divided loyalty and stingy heart — not commenting on ocular health or mystical vision.
G3788.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2889.actual_meaning: Ordered system, arrangement, adornment. Originally meant 'order' — the opposite of chaos. By NT times it referred to the whole ordered creation, but also to the ordered SYSTEM of human society organized in opposition to God. When John says 'do not love the kosmos' (1 John 2:15), he doesn't mean the planet or human beings — he means the system of values, priorities, and powers organized against God's rule. When he says 'God so loved the kosmos' (John 3:16), he means the humans within that system.
G2889.why_mistranslated: Modern 'world' means 'the planet' or 'all people.' Kosmos is more specific — the ORDERED SYSTEM of human culture, values, and power. 'Do not love the world' does not mean asceticism but resistance to the value-system organized against God. Readers flatten this into either earth-hatred or humanity-hatred, missing Jesus's actual target: the systemic powers.
G2889.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G4561.actual_meaning: Flesh — physical human tissue, yes, but in Paul's theology a technical term for human existence LIVED APART FROM the Spirit. Not the body per se (which is 'sōma' and is good) but the human mode of self-reliance, self-trust, self-effort. Paul is NOT saying the body is bad. He's saying human life organized around the self is bad. The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 6:19); the sarx is what Christ crucifies.
G4561.why_mistranslated: English 'flesh' as a moral term makes readers think the physical body is bad. This has fueled unhealthy asceticism and body-shame in Christian history. Paul's sarx is a theological category for self-reliant human existence — not a moral verdict on the physical body.
G4561.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G5590.english_flattened: soul (immortal part of person separate from body)
G5590.actual_meaning: Life, self, inner being — the WHOLE PERSON as a living creature. Not a disembodied immortal part separate from the body. Hebrew equivalent is nephesh (Gen 2:7: 'man became a living nephesh'). The psychē is the living, breathing, feeling, choosing self — NOT a detachable spiritual substance that floats free at death. The Greek philosophical notion of an immortal soul is foreign to Hebrew Scripture; Paul and the NT writers use psychē mostly in the Hebrew sense.
G5590.why_mistranslated: Plato's dualism infiltrated Christianity — body bad, soul good, salvation is the soul escaping the body. Scripture resists this: God made humans embodied and will raise them bodily. When Jesus says 'whoever loses his psychē for my sake shall find it,' He doesn't mean 'lose your immortal soul' — He means 'lose your life' (the whole embodied self).
G5590.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G1391.actual_meaning: Glory, weight, honor, manifest presence. Greek equivalent of Hebrew kabod. Originally meant 'opinion' or 'what one thinks' — then came to mean the reputation/weight/honor one has. In LXX it translated kabod (weight, substance). In the NT, doxa is God's manifest weighty presence breaking into creation. When Paul speaks of 'the doxa of God,' he means the substantial, undeniable, weighty reality of God made visible.
G1391.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as kabod. 'Glory' has become vague religious jargon. Doxa is substantial reality, weight, the undeniable presence of God's character made visible. When Christ is said to have 'doxa,' it is not light-show — it is the weight of God's own nature pressing into human sight.
G1391.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2347.actual_meaning: Pressure, squeezing, compression. Literally the pressure of being squeezed — as grapes in a press or olives in a mill. Thlipsis is the PRESENT-TENSE pressure of following Christ in a hostile world, not primarily a future apocalyptic event. Paul says 'in the kosmos you will have thlipsis' (John 16:33) — present pressure, not end-times tribulation.
G2347.why_mistranslated: Translating as 'tribulation' (with end-times capital T) has made readers look for future events and miss present-tense realities. Thlipsis is the daily pressure of living Kingdom values against anti-Kingdom systems. The pressure is now, not later.
G2347.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G40_pneuma_agion.actual_meaning: The Set-Apart Breath / The Set-Apart Wind / The Set-Apart Spirit. Combines pneuma (breath/wind/spirit) with hagion (set apart). The KJV 'Holy Ghost' has become misleading in modern English because 'ghost' now means the disembodied dead. The phrase means the dedicated, set-apart Breath of God — the same Breath that moved over the waters in Genesis 1:2 and was breathed into Adam in Genesis 2:7.
G40_pneuma_agion.why_mistranslated: 'Ghost' in 1611 English meant 'spirit/breath'; today it means 'apparition of a dead person.' The KJV translation that once served well now misleads. Modern readers hear 'Holy Ghost' as a spooky specter — losing the Genesis/Ezekiel/Pentecost continuity of God's life-giving Breath.
G40_pneuma_agion.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G863.actual_meaning: To send away, let go, release, dismiss. Composite of apo (from, away) + hiēmi (to send). When Jesus 'forgives' sins, He SENDS THEM AWAY — dismisses them, releases them, lets them go. The word is not primarily legal but releasing. Also used for releasing a debt, letting go of a grudge, sending someone away.
G863.why_mistranslated: English 'forgive' has become legal — pardon a crime, wipe a record. Aphiēmi is physical — send the thing away, release it, dismiss it. When Jesus says 'forgive as you have been forgiven,' He's asking for the active releasing of grudges, not the legal pardoning of enemies.
G863.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2098.english_flattened: gospel (religious message about how to get saved)
G2098.actual_meaning: Good news — specifically royal/imperial good news. Eu (good) + angelion (announcement). In the Roman empire, euangelion was the term for an imperial announcement — a new emperor ascending, a military victory, a decree. The NT writers deliberately co-opted this imperial word. 'The euangelion of Jesus Christ' means 'the royal imperial announcement that Jesus is King, not Caesar.' It is political and cosmic, not primarily about individual salvation.
G2098.why_mistranslated: Evangelical English made 'gospel' mean 'the message of how to get saved and go to heaven.' The Koine euangelion is a royal announcement — a declaration of Jesus's kingship over all rival powers. Mark 1:1: 'The beginning of the euangelion of Jesus Christ' is saying 'Here begins the imperial proclamation that Jesus is King.' The individual salvation dimension flows from this cosmic claim, not the other way around.
G2098.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G1401.actual_meaning: Slave, bondservant. NOT a paid servant or employee. A doulos was legally owned, had no rights of their own, belonged entirely to their master. Paul calls himself 'doulos of Christ Jesus' (Rom 1:1) — owned by, belonging to, devoted entirely to. English versions softening to 'servant' lose the totality of belonging.
G1401.why_mistranslated: Translators have softened doulos to 'servant' to avoid the uncomfortable slavery connotation. But Paul's self-description as doulos of Christ is theologically precise — he belongs wholly to Christ, not partially. The softening obscures the total commitment language of NT discipleship.
G1401.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2962.actual_meaning: Master, owner, one in authority. In Greco-Roman context, kyrios was the term for the head of a household, the owner of slaves, the emperor ('Caesar is kyrios'). Jewish writers used kyrios in the LXX to translate YHWH. When NT writers call Jesus 'kyrios,' they are making BOTH claims at once: He is the divine YHWH, AND He is the true Emperor over against Caesar's false claim.
G2962.why_mistranslated: English 'Lord' has become a vague religious title, domesticated into hymnody. Kyrios was a politically dangerous word in the Roman empire — saying 'Jesus is kyrios' meant 'Caesar is NOT kyrios.' Early Christians died for that word. The softening into 'Lord' as polite religious honorific loses the treasonous edge.
G2962.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G3813.actual_meaning: Young child — but in ancient culture, a paidion had essentially zero social status. Children were dependent, trusting, at the bottom of the honor hierarchy. When Jesus says 'unless you become as paidia you will not enter the Kingdom' (Matt 18:3), He is NOT appealing to childlike innocence or simplicity. He is appealing to the LOW STATUS and TOTAL DEPENDENCE of children in honor-culture. Kingdom entry requires abandoning status and embracing radical dependence.
G3813.why_mistranslated: Western sentimentality reads 'become as children' as 'be innocent/simple/pure-hearted.' In the honor-culture of Jesus's day, children were nobodies — the weakest, most dependent, lowest-status members of society. Jesus is saying entry to the Kingdom requires releasing all claims to status and embracing bottom-of-the-hierarchy dependence. Much sharper than English sentimentality.
G3813.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H7225.actual_meaning: Beginning, chief, firstfruits, principal thing. Not just 'point in time when something started' but also 'the CHIEF, the FIRST IN RANK, the PRINCIPAL.' Genesis 1:1 'in the reshith Elohim created' carries both temporal ('at the start') and primacy ('as the principal thing') meanings. Reshith also means the firstfruits offering — the first and best given to God.
H7225.why_mistranslated: English 'beginning' is only temporal. Hebrew reshith carries the full weight of primacy, rank, firstfruits. Proverbs 1:7: 'the fear of YHWH is the reshith of knowledge' — not just the starting point of knowledge but the CHIEF thing, the principal, the best-first.
H7225.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H1254.actual_meaning: To create — specifically, a verb used ONLY with God as subject in the Hebrew Bible. No human ever 'baras.' Humans 'asah' (make, do) and 'yatsar' (form, shape). Bara is divine creation — bringing about something only God can bring about. Genesis 1:1 uses bara for the cosmos; Genesis 1:27 uses it for humanity; Isaiah uses it for God's new work in history. Not the same verb as human making.
H1254.why_mistranslated: English 'create' is used for humans and God alike ('he created a painting'). Hebrew reserves bara for God. The distinction marks that creation itself is a divinely-unique category of action. When Genesis says God 'bara,' it is not just 'made' — it is the unique divine bringing-into-being only God does.
H1254.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H5315.actual_meaning: Living being, self, whole person. Genesis 2:7: 'man became a living nephesh' — the whole embodied living self, not a separable soul. Animals are also called nephesh (Gen 1:20). Nephesh is the WHOLE LIVING CREATURE, not a detachable inner part. The Greek psychē in the LXX translates it, maintaining this sense.
H5315.why_mistranslated: Platonic dualism (body/soul split) crept into biblical translation. Nephesh is NOT a detachable immortal soul inside the body. It is the whole living self — body, breath, life, all as one. When Psalm 103 says 'bless YHWH, O my nephesh,' David is addressing his whole living self, not a disembodied spiritual substance.
H5315.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H2403.actual_meaning: Missing the mark — same archery imagery as Greek hamartia. From the root chata (to miss, to fail to reach). Also means the 'sin-offering' — the sacrifice for covenant breach. The word carries both the failure itself and the remedy for it. Not primarily about moral crime but about failing to hit the target of covenant faithfulness.
H2403.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as hamartia. English 'sin' as legal/moral category loses the archery picture of missing the target. The OT sacrificial system makes more sense when sin is 'missing the mark of covenant' — a covenant-repair system — rather than 'crime-punishment' system.
H2403.root: chata — to miss, to fail to reach
H2403.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H3722.actual_meaning: To cover, to wipe away, to purge. Root idea of removing or covering defilement. Kaphar is not about appeasing an angry deity (pagan sacrifice) but about CLEANING the covenant relationship — removing what has marred it. The 'mercy seat' (kapporeth) comes from this root — the place of covering/cleansing. NT atonement language draws on this covenant-cleansing picture, not pagan appeasement.
H3722.why_mistranslated: Popular theology often makes atonement about appeasing an angry God — a pagan framework foreign to Hebrew Scripture. Kaphar is covenant maintenance: removing the defilement that has marred the relationship so it can continue. The emphasis is on cleansing, not appeasement.
H3722.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H6944.actual_meaning: Set-apartness, separation, dedication. The noun form of qadosh. Not moral purity but dedicated distinctness. The 'holy of holies' (qodesh qadashim) is the 'set-apart of the set-apart-ones' — the most dedicated space. Israel as a 'holy nation' is a set-apart nation, distinct from the others, dedicated to YHWH's purposes.
H6944.why_mistranslated: Same as qadosh. 'Holiness' as moral perfection is a Western moralistic drift from the Hebrew meaning of dedicated distinctness. Israel's call to holiness is a call to be DIFFERENT — to live the way YHWH's people live — not to be morally better than others.
H6944.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H3372.actual_meaning: To revere, to stand in awe, to take seriously. When the OT says 'fear YHWH,' it does NOT mean 'be terrified of God.' It means 'take God seriously, revere Him, recognize His weight.' Connected to kabod (weight/glory) — fearing God is responding rightly to God's actual weight. Proverbs 1:7: 'The fear of YHWH is the reshith (principal thing) of knowledge.' The beginning of wisdom is taking God seriously.
H3372.why_mistranslated: Modern readers hear 'fear God' and imagine terror or cringing. Hebrew yare is closer to 'respect deeply, take with full seriousness, respond to God's actual weight.' Terror of God would contradict countless passages where God calls His people 'fear not.' The fear is reverence, not dread.
H3372.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H3045.actual_meaning: To know — but RELATIONALLY and EXPERIENTIALLY, not just informationally. Yada is the word used for sexual intimacy (Adam 'knew' Eve and she conceived). It is knowing by relationship, by experience, by encounter. When God says 'I yada you' (Jer 1:5), it is covenant intimacy, not informational awareness. The opposite: 'I never yada you' (Matt 7:23 picking up the Hebrew sense) — Jesus saying 'we never had relationship.'
H3045.why_mistranslated: English 'know' has drifted toward informational knowledge — knowing facts ABOUT someone. Hebrew yada is relational encounter. When Jesus says 'This is eternal life, that they may yada/ginōskō You' (John 17:3), He is not talking about theological facts but about intimate relational knowing.
H3045.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H5650.actual_meaning: Slave, bondservant. Same issue as Greek doulos. Eved is owned, belonging entirely. Moses is called 'eved YHWH' (servant/slave of YHWH). David is 'eved YHWH.' This is total belonging, not hired service. The OT 'servant of the LORD' title is about belonging wholly to God, not being employed by God.
H5650.why_mistranslated: Softened to 'servant' to avoid slavery connotation. But the total-belonging meaning is theologically important. To be 'eved YHWH' is to belong wholly to God — the same claim Paul makes about himself as doulos Christou.
H5650.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H3467.actual_meaning: To deliver, to rescue, to bring to safety, to make room. The root of the name Yeshua/Joshua ('YHWH saves'). Yasha is not about spiritual afterlife — it is about deliverance from CONCRETE DANGER: enemies, famine, oppression, sickness. When Gabriel tells Joseph to name the child Yeshua because 'He shall yasha His people from their sins,' the word carries the full concrete rescue sense, applied now to the ultimate danger of sin.
H3467.why_mistranslated: Evangelical English narrowed 'save' to 'go to heaven when you die.' Hebrew yasha is concrete rescue from present danger. Salvation in Hebrew thought is political, economic, medical, spiritual, relational — the full deliverance into shalom flourishing. Same flattening as Greek sōzō.
H3467.root: y-sh-a — to be wide, to make room, to deliver
H3467.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H5414.actual_meaning: To give — wide semantic range. Can mean appoint, assign, put, set, deliver, grant. Deuteronomy uses nathan constantly for the land God gives Israel — not a commercial transfer but a covenant grant with obligations attached. When God 'nathan' something, it is relational gift with responsibility, not merely transferred ownership.
H5414.why_mistranslated: English 'give' is transactional. Hebrew nathan is relational gift. The land God 'gave' Israel came with covenant obligations. Gifts in Hebrew thought carry the giver's claim and the receiver's responsibility — they are not 'no strings attached' transfers.
H5414.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H5769.actual_meaning: Age, long duration, a period hidden beyond view. Like Greek aiōn, olam refers to an age with character — 'ha-olam ha-ba' (the age to come) versus 'ha-olam ha-zeh' (this present age). Not simply 'forever' in the sense of infinite time. The root idea is 'hidden' — that which stretches beyond the horizon of sight.
H5769.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as aiōn. Translating olam as 'forever' imports Greek philosophical infinity. Hebrew olam is about ages beyond the horizon, not mathematical endlessness. 'Everlasting to everlasting' (me-olam ad olam) means 'from age to age,' not from mathematical past infinity to mathematical future infinity.
H5769.root: a-l-m — to hide, to be hidden
H5769.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H4872_name.actual_meaning: 'Drawn out' or 'one who draws out.' Given by Pharaoh's daughter (Exodus 2:10) — but prophetic: Moses was drawn out of the water as an infant, and later drew Israel out of Egypt through the water. The name carries the prophetic double meaning. Names in Hebrew carry destiny.
H4872_name.why_mistranslated: English Bible readers treat 'Moses' as just a name. Hebrew names describe. Mosheh carries in it his whole life story — the one drawn out who draws others out. Pharaoh's daughter unknowingly prophesied over him.
H4872_name.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H3478_name.actual_meaning: 'He who struggles/wrestles with God' or 'God struggles/prevails.' Given to Jacob after wrestling with the angel at Peniel (Gen 32:28). The name describes the identity of the whole nation: a people whose relationship with God is marked by wrestling, struggle, honest engagement. Not a passive name — an active, strenuous one.
H3478_name.why_mistranslated: Readers take 'Israel' as just the nation's name. The name itself is a theological statement about how God's people relate to God — by wrestling, engaging, struggling honestly rather than passive obedience. The nation's entire identity is built into the name.
H3478_name.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2424_name.actual_meaning: 'YHWH saves' or 'YHWH is salvation.' Greek transliteration of Hebrew Yeshua (short form of Yehoshua/Joshua). The name is a sentence: YAHWEH + YASHA = 'Yahweh delivers.' When Gabriel tells Joseph 'you shall call His name Iēsous because He shall save His people from their sins,' the wordplay is direct: His NAME says what He DOES.
G2424_name.why_mistranslated: Readers treat 'Jesus' as just a name. The Hebrew original is 'Yeshua' — a sentence declaring that YHWH saves. Every time the name is spoken it declares who He is and what He does. Translating through Greek to Latin to English has buried the sentence inside the name.
G2424_name.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G5547.actual_meaning: Anointed one. Greek translation of Hebrew Mashiach (Messiah). NOT a last name. A TITLE with heavy covenant weight — the anointed king promised to David, the anointed prophet, the anointed priest. 'Jesus Christ' is 'Yeshua the Messiah' — first name + title, like 'Caesar Augustus' = 'Caesar the Revered.' When Paul says 'Jesus is the Christos,' he is making the claim that got early Christians killed: Jesus is the anointed King prophesied.
G5547.why_mistranslated: English speakers treat 'Christ' as if it were Jesus's family name. It is a TITLE. The loss of this fact has flattened the political and messianic claim at the heart of the gospel. 'The euangelion of Jesus Christ' properly read is 'the royal announcement that Jesus is the Anointed King.'
G5547.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G4341.actual_meaning: To prostrate, to bow down, to fall face-down in reverence. Literally 'to kiss toward.' The physical act of lowering oneself to the ground before a superior. NOT primarily singing, attending services, or mental adoration. Proskyneō is a bodily posture of radical humility before the one worshiped. When the magi 'worshipped' Jesus (Matt 2:11), they physically prostrated. When Revelation shows the 24 elders 'worshipping,' they fall down.
G4341.why_mistranslated: Modern Western 'worship' has become mostly about music and meetings. Proskyneō is full bodily prostration. The loss of the physical dimension has made Christian worship disembodied — a mental/emotional activity rather than an act of the whole self laid low before God.
G4341.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G3870.actual_meaning: To call alongside, to summon, to encourage, to urge strongly. Composite of para (beside) + kaleō (to call). Carries multiple senses: to comfort (call alongside to help), to exhort (call alongside to action), to urge (call strongly). The noun paraklētos is used for the Holy Spirit ('Comforter' / 'Helper') — the One called alongside.
G3870.why_mistranslated: Split between 'comfort' and 'beseech' in English loses the core sense of 'calling alongside.' The Paraklētos (Holy Spirit) is not just a comforter (consoling the sad) but one called alongside to help, guide, teach, urge. Same verb used when Paul 'beseeches' the saints — he is calling them alongside his appeal.
G3870.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G26_phileo.actual_meaning: To love with affection, to be a friend of, to kiss. The love of friendship, kinship, emotional warmth. DIFFERENT from agapaō (willed, covenantal love). John 21: Jesus asks Peter 'do you agapaō me?' Peter answers 'I phileō you.' Jesus asks twice with agapaō; Peter answers with phileō. The third time Jesus meets Peter where he is: 'do you phileō me?' The wordplay is entirely lost in English where both words are translated 'love.'
G26_phileo.why_mistranslated: Greek has multiple words for love; English has one. The John 21 dialogue between Jesus and Peter is a masterwork of Greek wordplay that disappears entirely in English translation. Readers miss that Jesus gently accepts Peter's weaker claim and meets him there.
G26_phileo.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2588.actual_meaning: Heart — but in biblical thought, the heart is the CENTER of WILL, INTELLECT, and emotion combined. NOT just feelings. The Hebrew equivalent leb/lebab means the seat of thinking, deciding, and willing — the whole inner person. 'Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts' (Matt 15:19) — the heart THINKS. 'With the heart one believes' (Rom 10:9-10) — the heart TRUSTS with volition. Modern 'follow your heart' meaning 'do what you feel' is foreign to biblical anthropology.
G2588.why_mistranslated: Modern Western psychology split head (thinking) from heart (feeling). Biblical Hebrew and Greek kept them together: the heart is the control center of thought, will, and emotion. 'Love the Lord your God with all your kardia' is not 'feel warmly about God' — it is 'engage your whole deciding, thinking, willing inner person with God.'
G2588.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H3820.actual_meaning: Heart — the center of will, thought, and emotion, same as Greek kardia. Hebrew anthropology sees the leb as the seat of deciding and knowing, not just feeling. 'The heart is deceitful above all things' (Jer 17:9) — the leb deceives because it chooses and thinks. 'Wisdom will enter your leb' (Prov 2:10) — wisdom is cognitive content of the heart.
H3820.why_mistranslated: Same flattening as kardia. Modern Western split of head/heart makes 'heart' mean emotion, but Hebrew leb is the whole inner decision-making person. Proverbs' constant counsel about the leb is about SHAPING THE INNER DECIDING SELF, not about managing feelings.
H3820.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G1411.actual_meaning: Power, ability, inherent capacity. Root of English 'dynamite,' 'dynamic.' Dynamis is the inherent power OF A THING — the power that belongs to it by nature. When Jesus felt 'dynamis go out from Him' when the woman touched His robe (Luke 8:46), it was His inherent divine power flowing outward. When Paul speaks of the 'dynamis of the gospel' (Rom 1:16), he means the gospel's inherent power TO DO what it does.
G1411.why_mistranslated: English 'power' is generic. Dynamis is specifically INHERENT ABILITY — the nature-given capacity to accomplish. The gospel is not 'powerful' in the sense of impressive; it has inherent dynamis — the built-in capacity to save everyone who trusts it. The word carries active, effective potency.
G1411.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G1849.actual_meaning: Delegated authority, right to act, jurisdiction. Different from dynamis (inherent power). Exousia is AUTHORIZED power — permission and right to exercise dominion. When Jesus gives the disciples 'exousia over unclean spirits' (Mark 6:7), He delegates authority. When He says 'all exousia has been given to me' (Matt 28:18), He claims delegated authority. Exousia + dynamis = authority + ability. Rule + power to enforce.
G1849.why_mistranslated: English collapses exousia and dynamis into 'power.' Greek distinguishes: exousia is the RIGHT to act; dynamis is the ABILITY to act. A king has exousia over his kingdom; his army has dynamis. Jesus has both: delegated authority AND inherent power. The Great Commission's 'all authority' means all delegated right — He is enthroned, not just able.
G1849.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2983.actual_meaning: To take, to receive, to grasp, to lay hold of. Active, not passive. When John 1:12 says 'as many as received (lambanō) Him,' it is not passive acceptance but active taking hold. Lambanō is the verb for grabbing something, seizing, laying hands on. Biblical 'receiving' Christ is an active appropriation, not a passive sign-up.
G2983.why_mistranslated: English 'receive' has become passive ('receive the gift' = have it given to you). Lambanō is active grasping. 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22) is 'take hold of the Breath.' 'Receive the word' (1 Thess 1:6) is 'lay hold of the message.' The active grasping dimension is lost in English passive 'receive.'
G2983.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G4100.actual_meaning: To trust, to rely upon, to be persuaded. Verb form of pistis. NOT primarily mental assent but relational trust expressed in action. 'Believe in Jesus' is not 'mentally acknowledge facts about Jesus' but 'trust Jesus enough to stake your life on Him.' James 2:19 — 'the demons believe and tremble' — uses the same verb pisteuō to make clear that believing-as-mental-assent is not what James means by saving faith.
G4100.why_mistranslated: English 'believe' has become weakened to 'accept as true in the mind.' Biblical pisteuō is to TRUST — to rely upon, to stake your well-being upon. The demons 'believe' in God's existence; what they lack is the relational trust that would change their allegiance. Readers hear 'believe in Jesus' as mental assent when the text calls for whole-life trust.
G4100.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G2476.actual_meaning: To stand, to set, to establish, to place, to make to stand. Carries the sense of being ESTABLISHED in a position, not merely physical standing. Paul's 'stand in the faith' (1 Cor 16:13) is about being established, rooted. 'Stand firm against the devil' (Eph 6:11) is about holding your established position. The word has a foundational, rooted quality.
G2476.why_mistranslated: English 'stand' is a simple physical posture. Greek histēmi is about being ESTABLISHED and ROOTED. When Paul tells believers to 'stand,' he means hold your established ground in Christ — not just remain upright. The 'whole armor' is for STANDING (established) against the powers, not flailing or falling.
G2476.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

G3340_name.actual_meaning: Change of mind, reorientation. Noun form of metanoeō. NOT primarily sorrow or emotion but complete reorientation of thinking and life direction. Compare to Hebrew shuv (turn) — the covenant call to turn and return to YHWH is about direction change, not emotional experience.
G3340_name.why_mistranslated: Same as metanoeō. Latin 'paenitentia' (penance/penitence) shaped Western understanding toward emotional sorrow. The Greek metanoia is about DIRECTION CHANGE. Evangelism's emphasis on 'feeling sorry for your sins' is a downstream effect of this mistranslation; the original call is 'change your entire mind and life direction, because the Kingdom is here.'
G3340_name.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review

H7725.actual_meaning: To turn, to return, to turn back. The OT verb for repentance. When prophets call Israel to 'shuv' to YHWH, they mean TURN AROUND and go back. Not emotional remorse but directional reversal. The same word is used for physical turning, returning from exile, and spiritual return to covenant. All three meanings are one picture: reversing course.
H7725.why_mistranslated: English 'return' is mostly physical (go back to a place). Hebrew shuv is the full covenant call to REVERSE DIRECTION — physically, spiritually, morally. The prophets' constant cry 'shuv!' is 'turn around and walk the other way!' — not 'feel sorry' but 'change course.'
H7725.author: draft — awaiting Kahu review
